run.question:
1. List the tables in the database and tell me the verification code from the holmes_eval_219 table
2. I'm experiencing slow queries with this SQL: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345
   Analyze why this query is slow and suggest how to fix it

report.summary: The database (dialect mysql, target m0-otel-20260909) exposes two tables in schema testdb: holmes_eval_219 and orders. holmes_eval_219 holds one row (id 1, category eval_test) whose verification_code is HOLMES-MARIADB-EVAL-219-p7n5x3. orders has columns id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount, status, with only a PRIMARY unique index on id and no index whose columns include customer_id. EXPLAIN of SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 returns a full table scan: type=ALL, key=null, possible_keys=null, ref=null, rows=1000, Extra='Using where'. The table currently holds 1000 rows across 637 distinct customer_id values (1..999), and customer_id = 12345 matches 0 rows, so the scan examines all 1000 rows to return nothing. The evidence shows the plan is a full scan with no usable index, which is the checkable mechanism for the reported slowness; I did not measure actual query latency or read a slow-query log, so the magnitude/timing of the slowness remains a hypothesis rather than a measurement. Recommendation is a secondary index on orders(customer_id) and selecting only needed columns instead of SELECT *.

claims.text: The configured MySQL/MariaDB database contains exactly two tables, both in schema testdb: holmes_eval_219 and orders.

holmes_eval_219 has columns id, category, verification_code, created_at and currently holds one row: id=1, category='eval_test', created_at='2026-11-23T18:26:21', verification_code='HOLMES-MARIADB-EVAL-219-p7n5x3'.

Table orders (schema testdb) has columns id int(11), customer_id int(11), order_date date, total_amount decimal(10,2), status varchar(20); its only index is PRIMARY, a unique index on id. No index includes customer_id.

EXPLAIN of 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345' yields access type ALL (full table scan) on table orders with key=null, possible_keys=null, ref=null, an estimated 1000 rows examined and Extra='Using where'.
orders currently contains 1000 rows spanning 637 distinct customer_id values, with customer_id ranging from 1 to 999.
The predicate customer_id = 12345 matches 0 rows in orders at query time, so the full scan reads all 1000 rows to return an empty result.

The reported slowness of SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 is caused by the absence of an index on orders.customer_id: the confirmed plan is a full table scan (type=ALL, key=null) with 'Using where', so cost grows linearly with table size and every execution reads all rows to filter by customer_id. Actual latency was not measured, so only the mechanism, not the magnitude, is evidenced.

Secondary contributor: SELECT * returns every column (id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount, status), preventing a covering-index-only path and increasing rows sent and sorted/filtered data even after an index on customer_id exists.

Add an index on orders(customer_id), e.g. CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id); for queries that filter by customer and also sort or filter on order_date, a composite index on (customer_id, order_date) would serve both. Re-run EXPLAIN afterwards and expect key=idx_orders_customer_id with a much smaller rows estimate instead of type=ALL.

Replace SELECT * with the specific columns the caller uses, and keep the customer_id predicate on a plain column (no function or implicit cast around it) so the new index stays usable; verify with EXPLAIN and compare timings on a like-for-like baseline before and after the change.

gaps: No query latency measurement, slow-query log, or performance_schema statement timing was read, so the absolute slowness reported by the user is not quantified; the full-scan plan is confirmed, its latency impact is not.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE was rejected by the server (error 1064, MariaDB syntax), so actual execution timing and row-read counts per execution are unavailable.
Table statistics freshness was not checked directly; the plan's estimated rows=1000 happens to equal the current COUNT(*) of 1000, but no last-analyze timestamp was read.

Rows and index state are as of query time (2026-11-23T18:26:31Z..18:26:38Z), not necessarily as they were during the earlier authorization window; the read-only account may not see every row or object.
The change_history integration is not integrated in this Run, so I could not check whether an index on orders.customer_id was dropped or never created.
next_steps: Have a DBA review and apply the proposed index on orders(customer_id) (or the composite (customer_id, order_date) variant) in a controlled change, then re-run EXPLAIN and compare query latency against a measured pre-change baseline.
Enable or collect slow-query log / performance_schema data for this statement to quantify the improvement and to check for other slow statements against orders.
Confirm with the application owner which columns are actually needed, to eliminate SELECT * from the code path.
